::: {.lead}
Today is presentation day. In Online activity 14 you planned your course
project, built the data sheet and wrote the first draft of the report. Now
you turn the report into **five slides**, **check** every slide, and
**present** your project in **three minutes**. Sami, a student, presents
the canteen sales of Sunrise Company; you present your own topic. In Online
activity 15 you finish the three files. Every section ends with a lab task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary presentation-outline slides-from-outline speaker-notes presenter-view ai-image check-ai-output ai-use-statement rehearsal >}}

## 10.1 From the report to five slides

A three-minute talk needs only **five slides** (@fig-five).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 10.1 — Five slides"}
1. **Title:** the topic and your name.
2. **Question:** your project question in one sentence.
3. **Chart:** the answer in a picture, with a title.
4. **Insights:** two short, checked sentences with numbers.
5. **End:** thanks, questions, and your AI-use line.

Make them fast from the report. In Word, give the five slide titles the
style **Heading 1** and close the file. In PowerPoint, choose **Home › New
Slide › Slides from Outline** and the report: each Heading 1 line becomes a
slide title. Or ask an AI tool for an outline of five slides from your
report (Online activity 10). Then copy the chart in Excel, paste it on
slide 3, choose a theme (Lecture 8), and write few words on each slide.
:::

![Five slides for a three-minute talk.](images/five-slides.png){#fig-five width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.1 — Sami's slides"}
1. Sami gives the five titles in the report the style Heading 1 and runs
   Slides from Outline.
2. On slide 3, Sami pastes the column chart of the total by item from
   Excel.
3. Slide 4 gets two insights: "Sandwiches earned the most: 138 JD." and
   "Tea sold the most cups: 150."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Copying whole paragraphs of the report onto the slides. The class reads
instead of listening. Put a few words on the slide and say the rest.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Your five slides"}
1. Make `talk.pptx` with five slides from your report (Slides from Outline
   or an AI outline).
2. Paste your chart from Excel on slide 3, and write two insights with
   numbers on slide 4.

*Your result:* `talk.pptx` with five slides.

::: {.check}
Five slides: the title with your name, your question, the chart with a
title, two insights with numbers, and the end. With the canteen data, for
example: "Sandwiches earned the most: 138 JD." and "Tea sold the most
cups: 150."

- ☐ Each slide has a few words, not a paragraph.
- ☐ The chart comes from your Excel file.
:::
:::

## 10.2 Check every slide

AI makes slides fast, and it can also make mistakes. Check every slide
before you present (@fig-checks).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 10.2 — Four checks"}
- **Accuracy:** every number on a slide is the same as in your Excel
  sheet.
- **Claims:** every sentence is shown by your data. "Sandwiches earned the
  most" is shown; "everyone loves sandwiches" is not.
- **Pictures:** an AI picture fits the topic, shows no wrong text, and
  shows groups of people fairly (Lecture 9).
- **Honesty:** the last slide says where AI helped (Lecture 9), and no
  slide shows personal data.
:::

![Four checks for every slide.](images/slide-checks.png){#fig-checks width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.2 — Two mistakes on Sami's slides"}
1. Slide 3 says "Total: 451 JD". Excel says 415 JD: two digits were
   swapped. Sami corrects the text.
2. The AI wrote "Everyone loves sandwiches." Sami changes it to
   "Sandwiches earned the most: 138 JD."
:::

{{< sim file="sims/deck-checker.html" poster="sims/deck-checker.png" title="Deck Checker: ready to present?" height="880" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Checking only the chart and not the text around it. A wrong number in a
sentence is as bad as a wrong bar.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Check your slides"}
1. In **Deck Checker**, mark Sami's five slides.
2. Check your own slides with the four checks, and fix every problem.

*Your result:* five checked slides.

::: {.check}
Deck Checker: slide 1 is OK; slide 2, the picture does not fit (a big
restaurant, not a small canteen); slide 3, a wrong number (451 JD, but
Excel says 415 JD); slide 4, a claim that the data does not show
("Everyone loves sandwiches"); slide 5, no AI-use line. Your slides: every
number as in Excel, every sentence shown by your data, pictures that fit,
and an AI-use line on slide 5.
:::
:::

## 10.3 Present in three minutes

A good talk is planned and practised (@fig-presenter).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 10.3 — Presenting"}
- Write short **speaker notes** under each slide: reminders, not a text
  to read.
- Start the slide show with **Presenter View** (Lecture 8): you see the
  slide, the next slide, your notes and a timer. The class sees only the
  slide.
- About **30–40 seconds per slide**. Do one **rehearsal** with a timer
  before your turn.
- Look at the class, speak slowly, and end with your main insight.
- Answer questions honestly. If you do not know, say so and say how you
  could find out.
:::

![Presenter View.](images/presenter-view.png){#fig-presenter width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 10.3 — Sami's three minutes"}
1. Sami's notes on slide 3: "Sandwiches earned the most: 138 JD. Tea sold
   the most cups."
2. In the rehearsal, the talk takes 4 minutes. Sami cuts one sentence on
   each slide: now it takes 3 minutes.
3. Someone asks: "Why did tea sell more cups?" Sami says: "My data does
   not show why. A short survey could tell us."
:::

{{< sim file="../week-09/sims/rehearsal-lab.html" poster="../week-09/sims/rehearsal-lab.png" title="Rehearsal Lab: Presenter View and the timer" height="760" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading the slides aloud with your back to the class. Use the notes in
Presenter View, and look at the people.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Rehearse and present"}
1. In **Rehearsal Lab**, rehearse Sami's talk once, with each slide close
   to its plan.
2. Write short speaker notes for your five slides, rehearse your talk
   alone with a timer, and write the time. Present it when the teacher
   calls you.

*Your result:* speaker notes and a talk of about three minutes.

::: {.check}
Rehearsal Lab: every slide says "about right", and the total is about
3:00 (the plan: 0:20, 0:45, 0:45, 0:45 and 0:25). Your talk: about three
minutes, 30–40 seconds per slide. Too long? Cut one sentence on each slide,
not the chart or the numbers.
:::
:::

## Case study: Presentation Day

On the day of the talks, six things happen: a rehearsal takes 4 minutes, a
slide has a claim that the data does not show, time runs out, someone asks
a hard question, a student reads every word, and the teacher asks if AI
wrote the insights. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these
situations. In the mini-game below you choose the best thing to do each
time.

{{< sim file="sims/presentation-day.html" poster="sims/presentation-day.png" title="Presentation Day: six situations" kind="game" height="460" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Six situations"}
Play **Presentation Day** (above) to the end.

*Your result:* your stars, and the two situations that were hardest for
you, with the right answers.

::: {.check}
The long rehearsal: cut one sentence on each slide. The claim: change it to
what the data shows. 2:40 and two slides left: say the main insight and
finish. The hard question: say so, and say how you could find out. Reading
every word: look at the class and use the notes. The question about AI:
say where AI helped and how you checked it.
:::
:::

View" and "Rehearse your slide show with Speaker Coach"
(support.microsoft.com).

## Exercises

1. Name the five slides of a three-minute talk.
2. How can you make the slides quickly from your report?
3. Name the four checks for every slide.
4. Excel says 415 JD; a slide says 451 JD. Which check fails?
5. Why is "Everyone loves sandwiches" a problem?
6. What must the last slide say when AI helped?
7. How long should each slide take in a three-minute talk?
8. What do you see in Presenter View that the class does not see?
9. What is a rehearsal?
10. What do you say when you do not know the answer to a question?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Title, question, chart, insights, end.
2. Give the titles Heading 1 and use Slides from Outline, or ask an AI tool for an outline of five slides.
3. Accuracy, claims, pictures, honesty.
4. Accuracy.
5. The data shows sales, not what everyone loves.
6. Where AI helped: an AI-use line.
7. About 30–40 seconds.
8. The next slide, the notes and a timer.
9. Saying the whole talk once with a timer before the real talk.
10. Say that you do not know, and how you could find out.
:::
